base_method_text.title: Accelerating Convergence of Score-Based Diffusion Models, Provably
base_method_text.summary:
Score-based diffusion models, while achieving remarkable empirical
performance, often suffer from low sampling speed, due to extensive function
evaluations needed during the sampling phase. Despite a flurry of recent
activities towards speeding up diffusion generative modeling in practice,
theoretical underpinnings for acceleration techniques remain severely limited.
In this paper, we design novel training-free algorithms to accelerate popular
deterministic (i.e., DDIM) and stochastic (i.e., DDPM) samplers. Our
accelerated deterministic sampler converges at a rate $O(1/{T}^2)$ with $T$ the
number of steps, improving upon the $O(1/T)$ rate for the DDIM sampler; and our
accelerated stochastic sampler converges at a rate $O(1/T)$, outperforming the
rate $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the DDPM sampler. The design of our algorithms
leverages insights from higher-order approximation, and shares similar
intuitions as popular high-order ODE solvers like the DPM-Solver-2. Our theory
accommodates $\ell_2$-accurate score estimates, and does not require
log-concavity or smoothness on the target distribution.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces novel training-free algorithms to accelerate both deterministic (DDIM) and stochastic (DDPM) score-based diffusion models, achieving improved convergence rates of O(1/T^2) and O(1/T) respectively, without requiring stringent assumptions on the target data distribution.
base_method_text.methodology: The approach leverages insights from higher-order approximation and momentum terms to adjust the update rule in discrete time. For the deterministic sampler, it shares similar intuitions with high-order ODE solvers like DPM-Solver-2. The stochastic sampler is designed based on higher-order expansions of the conditional density.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The proposed deterministic samplers were evaluated using pre-trained score functions from Huggingface on the CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, and LSUN-Churches datasets. The image quality was visually compared for different numbers of function evaluations (NFEs).
base_method_text.limitations: The convergence theory might be sub-optimal in terms of its dependency on the problem dimension. The deterministic sampler requires stronger assumptions on the score estimates.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research directions include refining the dimension dependency in the convergence theory, extending the algorithm and theory using ideas from third-order or higher-order ODEs, and designing higher-order solvers for SDE-based samplers.

add_method_texts.title: InstructVideo: Instructing Video Diffusion Models with Human Feedback
add_method_texts.summary:
Diffusion models have emerged as the de facto paradigm for video generation.
However, their reliance on web-scale data of varied quality often yields
results that are visually unappealing and misaligned with the textual prompts.
To tackle this problem, we propose InstructVideo to instruct text-to-video
diffusion models with human feedback by reward fine-tuning. InstructVideo has
two key ingredients: 1) To ameliorate the cost of reward fine-tuning induced by
generating through the full DDIM sampling chain, we recast reward fine-tuning
as editing. By leveraging the diffusion process to corrupt a sampled video,
InstructVideo requires only partial inference of the DDIM sampling chain,
reducing fine-tuning cost while improving fine-tuning efficiency. 2) To
mitigate the absence of a dedicated video reward model for human preferences,
we repurpose established image reward models, e.g., HPSv2. To this end, we
propose Segmental Video Reward, a mechanism to provide reward signals based on
segmental sparse sampling, and Temporally Attenuated Reward, a method that
mitigates temporal modeling degradation during fine-tuning. Extensive
experiments, both qualitative and quantitative, validate the practicality and
efficacy of using image reward models in InstructVideo, significantly enhancing
the visual quality of generated videos without compromising generalization
capabilities. Code and models will be made publicly available.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces InstructVideo, a novel approach to enhance text-to-video diffusion models using human feedback. It addresses the issue of visually unappealing and misaligned video generation by fine-tuning the models with reward signals derived from image reward models. The key contributions include reformulating reward fine-tuning as an editing process for efficiency, and using Segmental Video Reward (SegVR) and Temporally Attenuated Reward (TAR) to adapt image reward models for video.
add_method_texts.methodology: InstructVideo recasts reward fine-tuning as an editing procedure, using partial inference of the DDIM sampling chain to reduce computational costs. It employs Segmental Video Reward (SegVR) to sparsely sample frames for reward signals and Temporally Attenuated Reward (TAR) to weigh central frames more heavily, mitigating temporal modeling collapse. LoRA is used for efficient fine-tuning.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The experiments were conducted using the ModelScopeT2V model trained on the WebVid10M dataset. The prompts describing 45 animal species. HPSv2 was used as the primary reward model. Evaluation metrics included HPSv2 score and user studies to assess video quality and text alignment. Generalization was tested on new animal prompts and non-animal prompts.
add_method_texts.limitations: The paper mentions the risk of over-optimization during reward fine-tuning, which can degrade video quality despite increasing reward scores. It also acknowledges that specialized video reward models might outperform the repurposed image reward models. Additionally, the method's reliance on image reward models might not fully capture the nuances of video quality and temporal coherence.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include developing more advanced video reward models that capture human preferences for video as a whole and designing strategic mechanisms to identify and ameliorate over-optimization during reward fine-tuning. Also, it is expected to explore the adaptation to other reward functions.

base_experimental_code: The paper does not include a specific code implementation of the proposed algorithms. It refers to implementations of pre-trained score functions available in Hugging Face's Diffusers library.
base_experimental_info: The experimental setup involves using pre-trained score functions from Huggingface on datasets like CelebA-HQ, LSUN-Bedroom, and LSUN-Churches for visual comparisons of image quality at different NFEs. No specific training details or metrics are provided in the context.
new_method:
Below is an example of a genuinely new method (Step 3) that draws on ideas from both the Base Method’s higher-order/accelerated diffusion sampling and the Add Method’s reward-based partial-inference approach. It aims to mitigate one of the Base Method’s core issues—namely, its lack of adaptiveness to user or external feedback during accelerated sampling—while preserving its faster convergence.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Novel Method: “Reward-Guided Accelerated Editing (ReGAE)”
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1) High-Level Idea
ReGAE combines the Base Method’s accelerated sampling scheme (inspired by higher-order ODE solvers) with a reward-guided partial-inference loop (inspired by the Add Method’s idea of “recasting reward fine-tuning as editing”). Rather than running a full forward-and-reverse diffusion cycle every time user alignment (or any external reward signal) is desired, ReGAE intermittently “corrupts” and re-corrects the sample with guidance from a reward model, leveraging only a partial chain of steps. This preserves much of the Base Method’s reduced sampling overhead while enabling alignment in real-time.

2) Key Components
• Accelerated Diffusion Updates:
  – As in the Base Method, ReGAE uses higher-order expansions (akin to DPM-Solver-2) to achieve faster convergence (O(1/T²) for deterministic sampling, O(1/T) for stochastic).  
  – A momentum-like term carries forward estimate improvements to minimize the total number of function evaluations.

• Partial-Inference Editing:
  – Inspired by the Add Method’s approach of “recasting reward fine-tuning as editing,” ReGAE periodically intercepts the sampling trajectory.  
  – Instead of running the entire reverse diffusion from scratch, it “corrupts” the current sample slightly and then continues the next few steps, thereby integrating the feedback only through a short diffusion segment.

• Reward-Guided Alignment:
  – A reward model (trained or adapted from an image/video preference model) computes alignment scores (for instance, aesthetic quality or text prompt relevance).  
  – When the reward dips below a threshold, ReGAE triggers the partial-inference editing loop to correct the sample’s trajectory, thereby nudging it toward higher reward without restarting the entire sampling process.

3) Workflow Outline
a) Initialize sampling with the Base Method’s accelerated sampler.  
b) After every N steps (where N is chosen to balance overhead and feedback responsiveness), compute the reward score on the current sample.  
c) If the reward is above a threshold, continue with the next accelerated steps as originally planned.  
d) If the reward is below the threshold, partially corrupt the sample by adding noise (similar to an editing step), then run M accelerated steps (M < N) guided by the reward model’s gradient signal until the reward recovers.  
e) Continue until the final sample is generated or the target number of steps is reached.

4) Why This Method Is New
• It does more than just “tweak” the Base Method’s update rule. Instead, it fundamentally integrates a feedback-driven partial-inference loop within a high-order accelerated sampler.  
• The Base Method’s improvements to convergence speed remain in place, but now the generation can also be steered on-the-fly by an external reward signal, addressing alignment issues or user preferences.  
• Unlike the Add Method, which focuses on reward fine-tuning for large-scale text-to-video, ReGAE repurposes the partial-inference editing mechanism specifically to maintain accelerated sampling rates (rather than standard DDIM) and to allow dynamic mid-sampling corrections.

5) Potential Benefits
• Maintains faster convergence promised by the Base Method (fewer total sampling steps).  
• Improves adaptability by incorporating real-time or offline reward signals without having to do a full forward-backward diffusion loop each time.  
• Allows fine-grained control to steer sample generation toward desired properties or prompts while preserving the speed gains.

Overall, this new architecture—Reward-Guided Accelerated Editing—tackles the Base Method’s lack of alignment or feedback integration by weaving in partial-inference reward updates, all while upholding its accelerated convergence guarantees.
